source: Wisconsin Administrative Code chapter NR 40 (Invasive Species Identification, Classification and Control), Register November 2024 No. 827

plants.lookFor: A shrub or small tree whose leaves stay green late into fall. Clusters of black, pea-sized berries. Scratch the bark: it's orange inside.
plants.photoCredit: Photo: Robert Flogaus-Faust, CC BY 4.0, Wikimedia Commons
plants.why: Leafs out earlier than native species and produces toxic berries that alter soil chemistry, stopping native regeneration.

plants.lookFor: A shrub or small tree whose leaves stay green late into fall. Clusters of black, pea-sized berries. Scratch the bark: it's orange inside.
plants.photoCredit: Photo: Sigitas Juzėnas, CC BY 4.0, Wikimedia Commons
plants.why: Releases underground chemicals (allelopathy) that destroy beneficial soil fungi, effectively poisoning the roots of surrounding native plants.

plants.lookFor: Tall spikes of pink-purple flowers from late June to September, with stiff, square stems and leaves in pairs.
plants.photoCredit: Photo: George Chernilevsky, CC BY 4.0, Wikimedia Commons
plants.why: One plant can make millions of seeds, and it chokes the wetlands that ducks, frogs, and turtles need.

plants.lookFor: Flat-topped clusters of tiny yellow flowers on tall stems, with leaves split into toothed leaflets. Grows along roadsides and in fields.
plants.photoCredit: Photo: Силаева Татьяна Борисовна, CC0, Wikimedia Commons
plants.why: It takes over roadsides and prairies, and its sap can burn skin when the sun hits it.
plants.warning: Don't touch! The sap can cause painful burns and blisters in sunlight.

plants.lookFor: Tall, bamboo-like stems with big spade-shaped leaves, and plumes of tiny cream flowers in late summer.
plants.why: It grows so strong it can push up through pavement, and its thick patches crowd out plants along rivers.

plants.lookFor: Pink-purple, thistle-like flowers with black-tipped scales underneath, and gray-green, deeply cut leaves. Wear gloves: it can bother skin.
plants.photoCredit: Photo: Jasper Shide, CC0, Wikimedia Commons
plants.why: It takes over sunny, dry places like prairies and makes it hard for other plants to grow nearby.
It looks like a pretty wildflower, but it spreads into woods and crowds out native flowers.
Birds spread its berries everywhere, and it changes the soil in ways that help it crowd out prairie plants.
Its roots creep underground and pop up as big prickly patches that crowd out other plants.
Its big flat leaves smother the plants underneath, and it spreads from roadsides into prairies.

plants.lookFor: A small spiny shrub with tiny oval leaves in bunches (green or dark red) and bright red berries that last into winter. Cut stems are yellow inside.
plants.photoCredit: Photo: Sandy Wolkenberg, CC BY 4.0, Wikimedia Commons
plants.why: It forms thorny thickets that deer won't eat, and those thickets can be good homes for ticks.
This vine smothers other plants and tricks monarch butterflies into laying eggs where caterpillars can't survive.

plants.lookFor: Lacy, fern-like leaves that smell bad when crushed, umbrella-shaped clusters of small white flowers, and smooth stems with purple spots.
plants.why: Every part of this plant is very poisonous to people and animals.
plants.warning: Don't touch it and never eat it! Every part is very poisonous.

plants.lookFor: A very tall grass with blue-green leaves and big, fluffy plumes like feather dusters, tan to purple.
plants.photoCredit: Photo: Eppu, CC BY 4.0, Wikimedia Commons
plants.why: The non-native kind grows in tall, thick walls that take over wetlands, but a native kind looks similar, so experts need to check.
This vine grows super fast and can cover and smother whole trees.
This prickly vine grows very fast and smothers other plants under a blanket of leaves.
It spreads quickly across forest floors and crowds out wildflowers and baby trees.
This vine climbs over shrubs and small trees and blocks their sunlight.
It grows taller than a basketball hoop in thick patches that crowd out plants along rivers.
It carpets the forest floor in spring and crowds out native spring wildflowers.
